summary:
Sucre stands under the national framework of Colombia. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier judicial route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

The killing baseline a visitor here is assessed against is national. Hate crimes killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025. On 5 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek; she died the following afternoon of a second cardiac arrest and no one had been arrested in the case. Her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia, and killings of trans Colombians continued afterwards.

Organised armed-group targeting forms a second layer of risk. Colombia recorded 41 trans women killed in 2023 and a further eight between February and April 2024. In Caquetá, a department neighbouring Sucre's region, armed groups gave trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulated "social cleansing" flyers naming trans women and sex workers; trans women there have few options beyond sex work. An activist quoted in the investigation states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases rather than gender-motivated homicides.

Entry, premises and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016 and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country; same-sex spouses present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers to claim the same visa, healthcare, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises.
tangentialFactors:
Official protection machinery exists on paper while the killing rate continues to rise. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention.

The armed-group threat is documented in departments near Sucre rather than in Sucre itself. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Flyer campaigns in Caquetá announce a "social cleansing" of named categories, and Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men. Reporting on the Millerey case describes calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

The recording practice reported by an activist has consequences beyond any single case: if the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, national totals such as the 41 killings in 2023 and 13 in the first quarter of 2025 may understate gender-motivated homicides. Departmental breakdowns of those totals were not available in the sources reviewed for Sucre.
localsOnly:
Residents change their sex marker by signing a document before a notary, without judicial authorisation, medical examination or psychiatric assessment, and the resulting identification carries a "trans" or "non-binary" marker.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

Residents who are partners in a same-sex marriage hold equal inheritance, pension, healthcare and visa rights, and same-sex couples have been able to adopt since 2015. Local residents seeking a recorded transfemicide finding must contend with a prosecutor's office that, according to an activist quoted in the reporting, records such killings as ordinary cases.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Sucre-specific information was found in any source in this inventory. Whether trans killings, threat flyers, forced displacement or armed-group "social cleansing" campaigns have been documented within Sucre itself remains unresolved here; the figures cited are national, and the case material comes from Antioquia and Caquetá.

The departmental distribution of the 41 trans women killed in 2023, the eight killed between February and April 2024 and the 13 killed in the first quarter of 2025 is not sourced; the sources reviewed do not disaggregate by department.

Whether Sucre's notaries, police and health facilities implement the national marker-change procedure and the 2016 and 2018 decrees as written is unresolved. A comprehensive trans law reported as under legislative consideration in 2025 was not confirmed in this inventory, and its current status is not sourced.
